title: What one durable commit costs
subtitle: 2,000 random puts, one put per commit, 16 B keys and 100 B values, one run per row

rows.label: kvdb, no sync
rows.detail: p50 1.2 µs, p99 4.5 µs. Survives a process crash only. Load average 4.6

rows.label: kvdb, fsync
rows.detail: p50 24.0 µs, p99 37.3 µs. On macOS fsync does not flush the drive cache. Load average 4.6

rows.label: kvdb, F_FULLFSYNC
rows.detail: p50 4.01 ms, p99 5.00 ms. The only real barrier on macOS. Load average 4.3

rows.label: SQLite, synchronous off
rows.detail: p50 10.3 µs, p99 41.9 µs. Load average 4.3

rows.label: SQLite, synchronous full
rows.detail: p50 67.5 µs, p99 1.74 ms, fullfsync off. Load average 4.3

rows.label: SQLite, full plus fullfsync
rows.detail: p50 0.69 ms, p99 3.71 ms. Faster than one F_FULLFSYNC, so this is not a like for like comparison. Load average 4.3

caption: Each step down the durability ladder costs one to two orders of magnitude. The F_FULLFSYNC row is the drive flushing its own cache, about 4 ms per commit. SQLite's fullfsync commits finish faster than a single F_FULLFSYNC takes on this machine, so Apple's SQLite is probably issuing a lighter barrier, which I have not verified. Shared Apple M4 Pro at a 1 minute load average of 4.3 to 4.6, single runs, indicative only.
